en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra*, translated during the Later Han dynasty by an anonymous translator, as recorded in ancient catalogs.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
There was a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food with right mindfulness.

He saw a place where a new great dwelling had been built—a multi-storied pavilion, lofty and prominent, with doors and windows exquisitely carved and decorated, its walls perfectly aligned and orderly, free from wind and dust, and providing a barrier against both cold and heat.
When the Venerable Ānanda saw this, he immediately thought to himself:
"If a son or daughter of good family were to construct such a magnificent and beautiful hall and offer it to the Saṃgha of the four quarters;

or if, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, another son or daughter of good family were to enshrine a relic the size of a mustard seed and erect a stūpa as large as an *āmala* fruit, with a spire like a needle and a parasol atop it like the leaf of a jujube tree; or even were to fashion an image of the Buddha no larger than a grain of barley."
"Between these two merits, which is greater?

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having finished his almsround, returned to his dwelling, and after eating his meal, putting away his robes and bowl, and washing his feet, he went to where the Buddha was.
With single-minded reverence, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet; having sat to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This morning, I donned my robes, took up my bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.”

He saw a place where a new great dwelling had been built—a multi-storied pavilion, lofty and prominent, with windows and doors exquisitely carved and decorated, and walls perfectly aligned; it was free from wind and dust, and shielded against both cold and heat. He then thought:
"If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who could build such a wondrous and beautiful dwelling and offer it as a gift to the Sangha of the four directions;

or if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there were again a son of good family or a daughter of good family who would enshrine a relic the size of a mustard seed in a stupa as large as an *āmala* fruit, with a finial like a needle, and a canopy atop it like a jujube leaf; or even if they were to fashion an image of the Buddha no larger than a grain of barley."
"Between these two merits, which is the greater?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

Ānanda! It is for the sake of many people, for the sake of the peace and happiness of sentient beings, out of compassion for the world, for the sake of the great assembly, and for the great benefit of devas and humans, that you have questioned the Tathāgata on this matter.
Ānanda! Listen attentively and reflect upon this well!

The land of Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas in extent; it is broad in the north and narrow in the south, and the faces of its inhabitants are shaped like chariots. Suppose this land were completely filled with sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, hemp, and groves, so densely packed that there was no empty space and they appeared as a single mass.
Ānanda! All these grasses and trees have become human beings and attained the stages of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and pratyekabuddha.

Suppose there were a person who, for as long as they lived, provided all necessary requisites—robes, alms bowls, food and drink, bedding and seats, medicine, and dwellings—to them in full abundance; and after their parinirvāṇa, built a stūpa for each of them, and having erected each stūpa, made offerings and paid homage with incense, flowers, music, burning incense, ointments, powdered incense, banners, flags, and precious canopies, providing all such things in full.
"What do you think? Are such merits not indeed many?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
“Sugata! These sons and daughters of good family shall obtain great merit.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Setting aside this Jambudvīpa, there is also Aparagoyānī, eight thousand yojanas in extent, where the faces of the people are like half-moons; among those people, one likewise performs great meritorious deeds."

"Furthermore, Ānanda! Setting aside this Aparagoyānī, there is also Pūrvavideha, which is nine thousand yojanas in extent and where the faces of the people are perfectly round. Among those people as well, they all likewise perform great meritorious deeds."

"Furthermore, Ānanda! Setting aside this Pūrvavideha, there is also Uttarakuru, ten thousand yojanas in extent, where the faces of the people are square. Among those people, all likewise perform great meritorious deeds in this manner."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Śakra Devānām Indra’s Great Adorned Palace is exquisitely carved and engraved, subtle and marvelous. It has eighty-four thousand jeweled pillars, interspersed with celestial blue lapis lazuli and gold, forming a lattice that covers it entirely; golden sand is spread upon the floor, and wonderful sandalwood forms the balustrades."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

This Great Adorned Palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, has eighty-four thousand jeweled windows, likewise interspersed with celestial blue lapis lazuli and gold to form a lattice covering its top; it is strewn with golden sand and features sandalwood railings."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

In this Great Palace of Majestic Adornment belonging to Śakra, Lord of Devas, there are also eighty-four thousand windows made of celestial deep-blue jewels, exquisitely beautiful and adorned as described above."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

This Great Adorned Palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas, also has eighty-four thousand watchtowers and pavilions on all four sides, surrounded by various jewels; their ornamentation is likewise as described above."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who construct such a Great Palace of Grand Adornment as that of Śakra, Lord of Devas, and offer it to the Saṃgha of the four quarters;..."
"What do you think?
Would these sons or daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition, obtain great merit?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Very many!”
“Sugata! These sons and daughters of good family shall attain great merit.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Setting aside the merit of these four continents, and further setting aside the merit of Śakra-devānām-indra’s Great Adorned Palace—if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who constructed hundreds of thousands of billions of Śakra-devānām-indra’s Great Adorned Palaces and offered them to the Saṃgha of the four directions;

and if there were another son of good family or daughter of good family who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, raised a stūpa for a relic the size of a mustard seed, with a base as large as an āmalaka fruit, a spire like a needle, and a parasol atop it like a jujube leaf; or even if they were to fashion an image of the Buddha no larger than a grain of barley—the former merit, though complete, would not equal a hundredth part of this, nor a thousandth, ten-thousandth, nor even a hundred-thousand-ten-thousand-billionth part; it cannot be measured.”

Ānanda, you should know that these are the immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata: the portion of morality, the portion of concentration, the portion of wisdom, the portion of liberation, and the portion of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

The Tathāgata possesses immeasurable merit, including great supernormal powers, the transformations of the bases of psychic power, as well as the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā—such immeasurable merits as these."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Receive and uphold this sutra with careful attention.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"I have received the teaching,
World-Honored One!
What is the name of this Dharma?"
"How should we receive and uphold this within the Dharma of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This is named 'The Unprecedented Dharma,' the skillful means for all pure and wondrous Dharmas."

For this reason, I earnestly entrust you with this: you should repeatedly and extensively explain it in detail for the sake of devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others. You should establish it as the seed of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness and merit; all sentient beings who hear it shall enter into the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness and merit.
"By these causes and conditions, they shall be free from all afflictions and all shall attain Buddhahood.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus rejoiced and paid homage.
*Buddhabhāṣita-adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra* *Bhaiṣajyarāja Buddha* *Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva* *Bhaiṣajyasamudgata Bodhisattva* *Paramottaradevarāja Buddha*
